hints: Look carefully at the two curves, compare both the starting steepness and the final flat level for experiment 1 and experiment 2.
Experiment 2 starts steeper so it is faster, but it levels off lower so it makes less $\text{NH}_3$ at equilibrium.
For this exothermic forward reaction, think about which single change speeds particles up yet shifts equilibrium to the left to give a lower yield.
walkthrough:
**Read what the graph is telling us**

Look at slope for rate and plateau for yield. Experiment 2 has a steeper initial slope but a lower final plateau than experiment 1.

That means: rate in experiment 2 > rate in experiment 1, but equilibrium amount of $\text{NH}_3$ in experiment 2 < in experiment 1.

**Recall the reaction features**

The equation is:
$$\text{N}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g}) \quad \Delta H = -92 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Forward reaction is exothermic and goes from 4 moles of gas to 2 moles of gas. So higher pressure favours more $\text{NH}_3$, lower pressure favours less. Higher temperature favours the endothermic back reaction, so less $\text{NH}_3$.

**Match faster rate with lower yield**

We need a change that makes collisions more frequent and energetic, but also shifts equilibrium left. Raising temperature does exactly that.

Higher $T$ gives particles more kinetic energy, so faster initial rate. But for an exothermic forward reaction, Le Chatelier predicts the equilibrium shifts left, so the final volume of $\text{NH}_3$ is lower. That matches experiment 2 perfectly.

options.A: A catalyst speeds up forward and back reactions equally by lowering activation energy. It would reach equilibrium faster but give the same final amount of $\text{NH}_3$. It cannot give a lower plateau, so this does not fit.
options.B: Helium is inert and does not take part in the equilibrium. It does not increase the rate in this way and does not shift the position to give a distinctly faster start with a lower yield. This is a distractor about inert gases.
options.C: Increasing pressure from 200 atm to 250 atm would increase collision frequency (faster rate) and shift equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas. That is to the right, giving more $\text{NH}_3$, so the plateau would be higher, not lower.
options.D: Raising temperature to 600 degrees C increases particle energy and collision success, so the initial gradient is steeper. Because the forward reaction is exothermic, higher temperature shifts equilibrium left toward $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$, so less $\text{NH}_3$ is formed at equilibrium and the plateau is lower. This matches both features of experiment 2.
